# How to Use Claude to Read Through a Long Rental Lease Before You Sign

> **In short:** Open Claude, paste the text of your lease, and ask it to pull out the key numbers — rent, deposit, repairs, notice period — in plain English. It can save you from missing a costly clause, but it can't replace a lawyer for anything truly high-stakes.

Signing a lease is one of those grown-up moments where a 30-page document lands in your inbox and somehow you still have to sign it by Friday. This guide walks you through using Claude, the AI assistant made by Anthropic, to turn that wall of legal language into a short list of things you actually need to know — like whether your deposit is refundable, who fixes the dishwasher, and what happens if you need to leave early.

## Before you start
- A free or paid **Claude** account at [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) (a free tier exists; longer documents may need a paid plan — Claude will tell you if so).
- A copy of your **lease as text** — either a PDF you can copy from, a Word doc, or an email body. Photos of printed pages won't work directly; you'll need the typed words.
- About **15 minutes** total: 5 minutes to copy the lease, 10 minutes to read Claude's summary and follow up.
- **One honest limit:** Claude can translate legal language into plain English and flag unusual terms, but it is not a lawyer. For anything involving large sums, unusual clauses, or disputes, pay a real legal professional.

## Step 1 — Open Claude and start a new chat
Go to [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) in your browser and sign in. Once you're in, look for a button that says **"New chat"** or **"Start a new conversation"** — usually at the top-left of the screen, often next to the Claude logo. Click it once. A fresh, empty chat window opens with a blinking cursor at the bottom. Starting a brand-new chat keeps Claude focused only on your lease, without old conversations mixed in.

If you've used Claude before and your screen opens straight into an old conversation, look for a small **pencil or "+" icon** in the left sidebar — that creates a new chat on desktop and mobile web. On the phone app, tap the speech bubble or **"New chat"** at the top. You'll know it worked when the message box at the bottom is empty and there's no previous conversation visible.
💬 Example: there's nothing to type yet — just confirm the new chat is open before moving on.

## Step 2 — Paste the full lease text into the message box
Open your lease document (PDF, Word, email, or webpage), select the entire text — `Ctrl+A` on Windows or `Cmd+A` on Mac — then copy it with `Ctrl+C` or `Cmd+C`. Click inside Claude's message box and paste with `Ctrl+V` or `Cmd+V`. A long block of text appears in the box. Before you hit send, scroll to the bottom of what you pasted and make sure it doesn't end mid-sentence — leases often have schedules or signatures at the end that matter.

If the lease is in a scanned PDF that won't let you select text, you can either type out the key sections by hand, open it in a tool that does OCR (text recognition — software that "reads" a scanned image and turns it into editable text), or ask your landlord for a Word version. On mobile, you may need to long-press and choose **"Select all"** before copying. You'll know it worked when the full document — including the end — is visible in Claude's message box.
💬 Example: you'll see paragraphs like "Tenant shall pay rent of $1,800 per month…" appear in your message box before you continue.

## Step 3 — Add the prompt that asks Claude to summarize it the way you need
Below the pasted text, in the same message box, type a short instruction telling Claude what you want. Press **Enter** to send. Within a few seconds, Claude starts writing a response — usually a section-by-section breakdown. Don't worry if it takes a moment; longer leases mean more to read.

If Claude says the message is too long, you've hit a **context limit** — the maximum amount of text it can hold in one chat. Split your lease into two parts (Section A, then Section B in a new message) and ask for summaries of each. On mobile, the send button looks like a small **paper airplane** instead of Enter. You'll know it worked when Claude responds with a clearly organized list of items from your lease.
💬 Example: "Here is my rental lease. Please summarize it in plain English. List: 1) total rent and when it's due, 2) the deposit amount and conditions for getting it back, 3) who is responsible for repairs, 4) the notice period if I want to leave, 5) any rules about pets, guests, or subletting, and 6) anything that looks unusual or risky for a tenant. Use short bullet points."

## Step 4 — Read the summary and ask follow-up questions
Read Claude's answer slowly. Look for any number or rule that surprises you — a sudden "non-refundable" deposit, a 90-day notice period, a clause about waiving your right to repairs. If anything is unclear, type a follow-up question in the same chat and press **Enter**. Claude remembers the lease because it's still in the conversation, so you don't have to paste it again.

If a follow-up question feels important, ask it more than one way — for example, "Can the landlord keep part of my deposit for any reason?" and then "List every reason my deposit might not be returned." Different framings can surface different answers. If Claude's answer is vague, ask "What does the lease actually say, word for word?" You'll know it worked when you can clearly explain each of the six points above to a friend in plain words.
💬 Example: "In plain English, what does the 'early termination' clause actually let me do — and what would it cost me?"

## Step 5 — Ask Claude to flag anything unusual or risky
Once you have the basic summary, send one more message asking Claude to play skeptic. Press **Enter** and wait for the response. This second pass often catches things the first summary smoothed over — for example, automatic rent increases, penalties for late payment, or a clause where you agree to something vague like "all reasonable costs."

If you're short on time, focus on what Claude flags as "unusual" or "worth checking with a lawyer" — those are the parts most likely to cost you money later. If Claude gives a clean answer and you feel comfortable, you're done. If not, the next step is to take that short list of concerns to a human. You'll know it worked when you have a list of 2–5 specific questions or worries you can act on.
💬 Example: "Now read the lease again like a careful friend. Point out anything that could be a problem for me as a tenant, especially fees, automatic changes, or things I'd have to pay for that I wouldn't expect."

## Step 6 — Save the summary somewhere you can find it later
Before you close the tab, copy Claude's summary and paste it into a document, email to yourself, or note-taking app. A lease dispute can happen months later — the day you move out, for instance — and you won't remember the summary then. Saving it now means you have your own plain-English record next to the original legal text.

If you're using a paid Claude plan, look for a **"Projects"** or **"Shared chats"** option in the sidebar; these can keep your lease conversation organized for later. On the free tier, the conversation may be deleted after a set period — don't rely on it as your only copy. You'll know it worked when you can open the saved note on your phone and see the key points: rent, deposit, repairs, notice, and any flagged risks.
💬 Example: paste the summary into a note titled "Apartment on Maple St — lease summary, 2026" so it's easy to find when you move out.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting only part of the lease.** Schedules, addenda, and signature pages often contain the real rules — especially about deposits and move-out conditions. If you paste a fragment, Claude will summarize a fragment.
- **Trusting the summary without reading the flagged items.** Claude is good at translating, but it's still a reader, not a lawyer. Anything it marks as unusual is worth a second look by a human professional before you sign.
- **Asking one giant question.** "Tell me everything" tends to produce a long, generic answer. Numbered asks — "1) rent, 2) deposit, 3) repairs…" — get you the specific facts you actually need.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Before you sign an apartment, a co-working space, a car lease, or even a phone-plan contract, the same trick works. Pasting the agreement into Claude and asking for a plain-English breakdown takes five minutes and often surfaces a clause you'd otherwise sign without reading.
- **For your business or work:** If you rent office space, equipment, or a venue for events, Claude can quickly compare two leases side by side. Paste each one into a separate chat, ask the same six questions, and see where the offers actually differ — because landlords usually don't tell you the differences themselves.
- **If you're just getting started:** The easiest first move is to pick one document you already have — your current lease, a job offer, or a subscription terms-of-service page — and run it through Claude today. Once you've done it once, the skill is yours for life.

## Try it now
Open Claude right now and paste the text of any agreement sitting in your inbox — a rental lease is ideal, but a gym membership or insurance contract works just as well. Ask for the same six-point summary, read the result, and see if anything surprises you. It takes about ten minutes, and you may spot something you'd otherwise have signed without noticing.
